Shark cage diving

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry keeping the town of Gansbaai on the map. We find out why for the first time in history are the shark nowhere to be seen.otry rthe

Unique Selling Point:
Shark cage diving attracts tourist from across the world to Gansbaai. Seen as the mecca of the Great White Sharks, Gansbaai is a unique spot for the Great Whites where food is readily available from the two small islands eight kilometres away. Sixteen years ago the first shark cage diving operator opened shop. Today there are eight operators running 3 boat trips every day. Until February this year shark cage diving generated in excess of R1 600 million every day. Recent sightings of a pair of Orcas and five dead sharks washed out on the beach has brought this industry almost to a halt. Studies have shown that the sharks now fear for their safety and have moved to safer waters. What does the future hold for Gansbaai and the shark cage diving boat operators and what has the economic impact been on every business, from the one man operator to the large operators who is have used this form of eco-tourism to fund valuable scientific and marine research.


Summary:
Gansbaai is the shark capital of the world for the Great Whites. With an estimated population of 1,500 sharks moving between the Cape waters and Mozambique, it was found that the majority of the sharks remained all year round in the Gansbaai waters. To study their movement in more detail, 38 Great White Sharks were tagged in 2012 with high tech satellite tags by a team of local and international marine biologists. They found the reason why so many Great White sharks are found around Gansbaai is due to the abundance of energy rich food readily available.

Eight kilometres off the coast of Gansbaai a strip of sea between two small islands that forms the perfect breeding ground for seals and penguins, two key food sources of the Great White shark’s diet. Each year roughly 60 000 seal pups are born on Geyser Rock island and on Dyer Island the penguins are protected as part of ongoing research studies.

Further information:
With almost a hundred percent guarantee of seeing these formidable creatures in their natural habitat, operators were able to sell tours with a smile. That is, until a few months ago when two things happened: the Great Whites went missing and at the same time Orcas, or Killer Whales were spotted in the bay. Killer Whales are rare visitors to these waters and never in recorded history have the Great Whites been so allusive.

Instead of the guaranteed shark sightings, the cage dive boats started returning to land with disappointed tourists on board and even refunding a portion of the fee they pay to see the Great Whites.

Then Alison Towner, a marine biologist who has been studying the Great Whites of Gansbaai for the last decade and was part of the tagging expedition in 2012 got a call from a local to tell her about a dead shark he found on the beach in Gansbaai. To her shock she found that it was one of the females that was tagged in 2012. But this was not the end. Within a matter of weeks, the same incident occurred four more times. A Great White found dead on the beach. The common denominator was that in each case only the shark’ liver was ripped from the carcass.

“It is the first time in recorded history that we have seen something like this. Five identical cases of sharks found dead on the beach with its livers missing.”

Alison identified three females of 4,9 meters and two males of 3,6 and 4,5 meters from the database tagging system. With the help of a team of experts, including dr. Malcolm Smale, Alison was granted permission by the Department of Environmental Affairs to dissect the sharks.


The Great White sharks have only one natural predator, the Orcas, or Killer Whales as they are sometimes referred to. The Orcas are part of the dolphin family and will feed on their own, as well as sharks, baby sperms whales, seals, penguins and large fish. The only part of a shark that the Orcas are interested in, is the rich liver and sometimes the heart. With no previously recorded attacks of the Orcas on the Great Whites in this area, the theory is that the unsuspected sharks have now become easy prey for the sharks of Gansbaai.

For Alison and the team of experts, they made history as it is the first time worldwide that Great Whites have been dissected after an Orca predation and it is also the first scientific observation of Orca killings on the Great Whites of South Africa.

But who pays for the science that takes place behind the scenes of marine biology? Tourists. Through eco-tourism, Marine Dynamics, the largest cage diving operator is able to employ 90 full time staff, including Alison’s salary, several other marine biologists, researchers, interns from across the globe, chefs who cook the meals for the tourist, and so the list goes on and on.

From the local B&B’s who provides accommodation for overnight tourists to the butcher selling the meat to the restaurants, to the small micro-enterprises like Martina who owns Sea View Cleaners, and want to know “when must I come and clean the windows again?, there is an industry that survives entirely on the sightings of the Great Whites in Gansbaai.

After a two day recci in Gansbaai and taking a trip myself out to Shark Alley, I witnessed the tangible disappointment of every single tourist on board who was hoping to see these magnificent creatures. They came from the Canary Island, Brazil, Switzerland, Germany, Missouri, to the far corners of Canada, each paying big money to come to the shark mecca of the world. There are only two other places worldwide where the Great Whites can be observed, but only in Gansbaai are tourist able to take a short trip out to sea and ‘with no previous experience’ and no scuba diving gear, are the young and old able to come within inches of the Great Whites.

But as we speak, the shark cage diving industry is in trouble. Since February this year, the cage diving boats have returned time and again without a single sighting of the Great Whites. One operator has told us that she has only had 230 cage diving trips in one season with very few sightings of sharks compared to the same time last year where she made 780 boat trips, where almost every excursion was a guaranteed shark cage dive.

On the window of the tourist shop it reads: Eight shark cage diving boats - three trips per day!
That would mount to 40 people per boat paying R1700 per person. Times that by eight boats three times per day and this small postage stamp in the small town of Gansbaai generates R1,632.00 per day.

Our story:
In our story we will go out to sea, interview the tourists to find out what they think, speak to the marine biologist about the science behind what is happening and talk to the boat concession owners who have lost major revenue and in some instances had to close shop.

We have footage of the necropsy and some visuals of the sharks during cage diving. However there is no footage available of a shark being attacked by an Orca as this is mostly happening at night. The story will be about the sharks moving away to safer waters and the direct impact it has had on the cage diving operators and the ripple effect on the industry as a whole.

Press Release:


Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry, bringing international tourists to the shores of Gansbaai, but for months, not a single Great White Shark could be spotted.
Instead, the carcasses of four Great Whites washed ashore. Tourism waned and businesses battled to survive. Why did the sharks disappear? Carte Blanche investigates.

Script:


Script: Shark cage diving
17 August 2017: FINAL

Up audio - “So surface temperature is 14.7, the pressure is 1029.”

V/O We’re off the Cape coast on route to Shark Alley, about eight kilometres from Gansbaai. It’s a hotspot for sharks, attracting 85 000 tourists every year.

Link: In the distance are Dyer Island and Geyser Rock. The latter with its massive population of seals, around 60 000, provides an ideal food source for Great Whites, and that coupled with a number of other environmental factors make this the shark cage diving capital of the world.

Up audio: ‘Now if those sharks do come up today we get our first group of divers in. Everyone ready?’

V/O On the boat the anticipation is palpable. Tourists are anxiously waiting to spot shadows under the water. Today marks 42 days since the last shark sightings. Some say a pair of Orcas have moved into the bay and are the reason the sharks have disappeared. But business has to carry on and so the boats go out and the tourists are hopeful.

John Webb: Why do you come to South Africa?

Karim: For wildlife, for landscape, for shark.

John Webb: Seeing sharks was one of the things you really, definitely wanted to do?

Karim: Yes, we hear it is the best place to see white shark but at this moment maybe there is a problem with the Orca.

V/O Orcas which are also known as Killer Whales, are the only natural predators for Great Whites. They are actually part of the dolphin family and are very clever and skilled hunters. They feed on baby sperm whales, will kill their own specie and even go for Great Whites.

Up audio: John coming out of the water.

Link: So while the sharks are absent this is effectively what the cage diving experience has become. Everybody quite literally is just holding their breath.

Wilfred Chivell: Shark cage diving operator: We say every day, today is the day. Today is the day, so yah, they must come back.

V/O Wilfred Chivell is one of the largest operators in town and he’s got reason to be concerned.

Wilfred Chivell: Shark Cage Diving Operator: Last year for the first time in 15, 20 years the sharks disappeared for a period of five weeks and we thought it is not the worst that can happen because they came back. And come this year in January they didn’t disappeared but in February they did, and then they came back and then in April they disappeared again.

V/O Charmaine Beukes has been running her company for eleven years and for the first time cancellations have become a reality.

Charmaine Beukes: Our policy is total honesty with our clients so we start the morning with 60 clients for the next day booked, our consultants are honest and tell them for how long we haven’t seen sharks and what the situation are and the next day we maybe go out with 15 clients.

John Webb: So when times were good how many boat trips did you do?

Charmaine Beukes: In summer season when it is light until late we do about 3 trips a day. So prior to this year we always would have said, well 99% of the time you will see a shark.

Link: If the weather plays along in Gansbaai shark sightings are almost guaranteed, hence signs like these. But sadly that is no longer the case and if the situation continues, these signs could be replaced by those.

Up audio: ping sounds

V/O Understanding the movements of the great Whites is essential for a sustainable business and eco-tourism. Alison Towner is a marine biologist and has been studying the Great White Sharks for the last ten years.

Alison Towner: Marine Biologist: We have been putting out acoustic receivers, acoustic tags, we have been looking at natural foraging behaviour, migration, where white sharks spend their time and there is such inconsistency in what they do.

V/O Around town there were rumours that Orcas were to blame for the shark’s disappearance. But without proof directly linking Orcas to killing the Gansbaai sharks, this remained a theory. Then, in the first week of May, Towner received a call from a local fisherman about a carcass on the beach.

Allison Towner: It was almost a five meter animal and she was very much dead. I think the initial feeling is complete and utter shock. You don’t expect to see something of that size washed ashore on the beach and our first thoughts were what could have been responsible for this?

V/O In one week four Great Whites were killed. The technique was the same - each shark was missing a liver. Towner feared that the two resident Orcas were responsible. To confirm her suspicions a detailed necropsy was conducted. Under the leadership of shark expert, Dr. Malcolm Smale three sharks were dissected.

Alison: The first thing we noticed of course is that she had a gaping wound on the underside of her under cavity and when we cut into the shark we found that her liver was completely absent. Experts in Orca research has described this sort of dexterity in other parts of the word and also the coordinated teamwork how one will hold the prey species while the other manipulated the part that they want. Notably with the three white sharks that washed up in sink each one had that characteristic laceration on the underside and just that liver gone.

John: It is noticeable that these sharks were large animals, animals is that unusual or not as far as the Orcas are concerned?

Alison Towner: I wonder if there hasn’t been some kind of shift in preference, you know the larger the shark the larger the liver and therefore the higher the nutrient payoff. A five
meter great white shark, female, her liver probably weighed at about 80kilos.

V/O After the killings in May the sharks simply vanished for three weeks. And every day the boats didn’t go out it cost money. For Kim Mclean this has been tough. She has cut her trips by half and refunds her clients 50% of their fee when no sharks are spotted.

John Webb: How are you able to keep your doors open?

Kim Mclean: Shark Cage Diving operator: I can honestly say it is tight. It is very tight. You can go back and get overdrafts and things to keep things going. My savings and things I have put back in just to keep the boat afloat so to speak. I don’t want to put my guys on short leave. I don’t want to say I have to retrench you. These are good guys. We spent also considerable amount of money training these guys.

V/O Sadly one operator had to close its doors. Odua Mpofu was a deckhand on their vessel.

John Webb: Why did it close?

Odua Mpofu: Retrenched employee: They said the company is bankrupt just because there is no sharks. That is the problem.

John Webb: No sharks no business.

Odua Mpofu: No business.

John Webb: And tell me how did you feel when they told you that? They said they are closing their doors?

Odua Mpofu: I was not alright. Did not feel ok because I have a lot of responsibilities, just because I am supporting my grandmother.

Up audio: natural sound

V/O Jurie Small was a videographer for the same company. He also lost his job.

Jurie Small: Retrenched employee shark cage diving charter: I had a full time job with a company. We work on what we sell, get paid for that on a commission basis so obviously if there is no sharks here that means no income. So it has a big effect on us.

John Webb: How long can you continue getting on the boat and not seeing sharks?

Jurie: Sooner or later I have to say I have a wife I have a child that I have to support. I have to go and find something else. I hope it is not going to happen I pray it is not going to happen but you have to face reality.

V/O The reality strikes a different cord with the employers who have to take care of their staff even during these difficult times.

John Webb: What would the impact be on closing your doors on the people you support with jobs?

Nick Walsh: Shark cage diving operator: This is what I have to deal with. This is my sleepless nights. I employ 25 people, they are all full time staff and those 25 people are the breadwinners for their families. So the ripple effect is going to be devastating.

V/O The Gansbaai community also relies on the cage diving business. Beukes runs a small recycle shop and a soup kitchen.

Charmaine Beukes: They bring their recyclables here. On a Tuesday we have about 240 children lining up all over the street coming with wheelbarrows with all their recyclables and if you have a little bag it gets you five points and then with five points you get a little card and that is our swop shop money you trade your card for something like school supplies.

John Webb: It is a wonderful idea.

Up audio: ‘Thank you very much get some soup’.

Up audio: ‘ And obviously the building..’

V/O With the income from the shark business Chivell was able to invest in marine conservation with projects such as the Dyer Island Conservation Trust and the Penguin Sanctuary. But without the financial inflows from the shark business Chivell had to take stock and diversify to whalewatching to keep his boat afloat.

John: And the impact on your business? It has been 5 or 6 weeks now, is it becoming a strain?

Wilfred: it is becoming a real strain, yes. If this carries on for another week or two I have to reorganise my business. It cant carry on like that. At least I have a whale watching business and I can carry some of the responsibilities of the shark to the whale watching business.

V/O When Great Whites sense danger from a new predator in the vicinity their natural response is to flee.

Alison Towner: It is very much a flight response and of course we don’t really know now how long it will take for the white sharks to sharks to be returning to the area.

V/O There has only ever been one recorded incident of a Great White being killed by an Orca. It was off the coast of California.

Alison: The fact is that we have not observed the live predation events here so the only evidence really that we have to relate to is off the western coast of California where 2 orcas were filmed extracting a white shark’s liver and in that situation what they sort of did was to bump it until they asphyxiated it and then they removed its liver.

V/O Just a few days after we left Gansbaai several Great White sharks were again spotted in the bay. For now business is back on its feet but with irregular sightings becoming more common, will the shark cage diving business be able to sustain itself?

Alison Towner: I just try and remain optimistic and I hope the natural balance will return. If it doesn’t we may as human beings really consider our impact on the ocean and what we can do to change that.

___________________________________________________________________________

references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 20 August 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 30 August 2017 Press Release: Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry, bringing international tourists to the shores of Gansbaai, but for months, not a single Great White Shark could be spotted. Instead, the carcasses of four Great Whites washed ashore. Tourism waned and businesses battled to survive. Why did the sharks disappear? Carte Blanche investigates. Script: Script: Shark cage diving 17 August 2017: FINAL Up audio - “So surface temperature is 14.7, the pressure is 1029.” V/O We’re off the Cape coast on route to Shark Alley, about eight kilometres from Gansbaai. It’s a hotspot for sharks, attracting 85 000 tourists every year. Link: In the distance are Dyer Island and Geyser Rock. The latter with its massive population of seals, around 60 000, provides an ideal food source for Great Whites, and that coupled with a number of other environmental factors make this the shark cage diving capital of the world. Up audio: ‘Now if those sharks do come up today we get our first group of divers in. Everyone ready?’ V/O On the boat the anticipation is palpable. Tourists are anxiously waiting to spot shadows under the water. Today marks 42 days since the last shark sightings. Some say a pair of Orcas have moved into the bay and are the reason the sharks have disappeared. But business has to carry on and so the boats go out and the tourists are hopeful. John Webb: Why do you come to South Africa? Karim: For wildlife, for landscape, for shark. John Webb: Seeing sharks was one of the things you really, definitely wanted to do? Karim: Yes, we hear it is the best place to see white shark but at this moment maybe there is a problem with the Orca. V/O Orcas which are also known as Killer Whales, are the only natural predators for Great Whites. They are actually part of the dolphin family and are very clever and skilled hunters. They feed on baby sperm whales, will kill their own specie and even go for Great Whites. Up audio: John coming out of the water. Link: So while the sharks are absent this is effectively what the cage diving experience has become. Everybody quite literally is just holding their breath. Wilfred Chivell: Shark cage diving operator: We say every day, today is the day. Today is the day, so yah, they must come back. V/O Wilfred Chivell is one of the largest operators in town and he’s got reason to be concerned. Wilfred Chivell: Shark Cage Diving Operator: Last year for the first time in 15, 20 years the sharks disappeared for a period of five weeks and we thought it is not the worst that can happen because they came back. And come this year in January they didn’t disappeared but in February they did, and then they came back and then in April they disappeared again. V/O Charmaine Beukes has been running her company for eleven years and for the first time cancellations have become a reality. Charmaine Beukes: Our policy is total honesty with our clients so we start the morning with 60 clients for the next day booked, our consultants are honest and tell them for how long we haven’t seen sharks and what the situation are and the next day we maybe go out with 15 clients. John Webb: So when times were good how many boat trips did you do? Charmaine Beukes: In summer season when it is light until late we do about 3 trips a day. So prior to this year we always would have said, well 99% of the time you will see a shark. Link: If the weather plays along in Gansbaai shark sightings are almost guaranteed, hence signs like these. But sadly that is no longer the case and if the situation continues, these signs could be replaced by those. Up audio: ping sounds V/O Understanding the movements of the great Whites is essential for a sustainable business and eco-tourism. Alison Towner is a marine biologist and has been studying the Great White Sharks for the last ten years. Alison Towner: Marine Biologist: We have been putting out acoustic receivers, acoustic tags, we have been looking at natural foraging behaviour, migration, where white sharks spend their time and there is such inconsistency in what they do. V/O Around town there were rumours that Orcas were to blame for the shark’s disappearance. But without proof directly linking Orcas to killing the Gansbaai sharks, this remained a theory. Then, in the first week of May, Towner received a call from a local fisherman about a carcass on the beach. Allison Towner: It was almost a five meter animal and she was very much dead. I think the initial feeling is complete and utter shock. You don’t expect to see something of that size washed ashore on the beach and our first thoughts were what could have been responsible for this? V/O In one week four Great Whites were killed. The technique was the same - each shark was missing a liver. Towner feared that the two resident Orcas were responsible. To confirm her suspicions a detailed necropsy was conducted. Under the leadership of shark expert, Dr. Malcolm Smale three sharks were dissected. Alison: The first thing we noticed of course is that she had a gaping wound on the underside of her under cavity and when we cut into the shark we found that her liver was completely absent. Experts in Orca research has described this sort of dexterity in other parts of the word and also the coordinated teamwork how one will hold the prey species while the other manipulated the part that they want. Notably with the three white sharks that washed up in sink each one had that characteristic laceration on the underside and just that liver gone. John: It is noticeable that these sharks were large animals, animals is that unusual or not as far as the Orcas are concerned? Alison Towner: I wonder if there hasn’t been some kind of shift in preference, you know the larger the shark the larger the liver and therefore the higher the nutrient payoff. A five meter great white shark, female, her liver probably weighed at about 80kilos. V/O After the killings in May the sharks simply vanished for three weeks. And every day the boats didn’t go out it cost money. For Kim Mclean this has been tough. She has cut her trips by half and refunds her clients 50% of their fee when no sharks are spotted. John Webb: How are you able to keep your doors open? Kim Mclean: Shark Cage Diving operator: I can honestly say it is tight. It is very tight. You can go back and get overdrafts and things to keep things going. My savings and things I have put back in just to keep the boat afloat so to speak. I don’t want to put my guys on short leave. I don’t want to say I have to retrench you. These are good guys. We spent also considerable amount of money training these guys. V/O Sadly one operator had to close its doors. Odua Mpofu was a deckhand on their vessel. John Webb: Why did it close? Odua Mpofu: Retrenched employee: They said the company is bankrupt just because there is no sharks. That is the problem. John Webb: No sharks no business. Odua Mpofu: No business. John Webb: And tell me how did you feel when they told you that? They said they are closing their doors? Odua Mpofu: I was not alright. Did not feel ok because I have a lot of responsibilities, just because I am supporting my grandmother. Up audio: natural sound V/O Jurie Small was a videographer for the same company. He also lost his job. Jurie Small: Retrenched employee shark cage diving charter: I had a full time job with a company. We work on what we sell, get paid for that on a commission basis so obviously if there is no sharks here that means no income. So it has a big effect on us. John Webb: How long can you continue getting on the boat and not seeing sharks? Jurie: Sooner or later I have to say I have a wife I have a child that I have to support. I have to go and find something else. I hope it is not going to happen I pray it is not going to happen but you have to face reality. V/O The reality strikes a different cord with the employers who have to take care of their staff even during these difficult times. John Webb: What would the impact be on closing your doors on the people you support with jobs? Nick Walsh: Shark cage diving operator: This is what I have to deal with. This is my sleepless nights. I employ 25 people, they are all full time staff and those 25 people are the breadwinners for their families. So the ripple effect is going to be devastating. V/O The Gansbaai community also relies on the cage diving business. Beukes runs a small recycle shop and a soup kitchen. Charmaine Beukes: They bring their recyclables here. On a Tuesday we have about 240 children lining up all over the street coming with wheelbarrows with all their recyclables and if you have a little bag it gets you five points and then with five points you get a little card and that is our swop shop money you trade your card for something like school supplies. John Webb: It is a wonderful idea. Up audio: ‘Thank you very much get some soup’. Up audio: ‘ And obviously the building..’ V/O With the income from the shark business Chivell was able to invest in marine conservation with projects such as the Dyer Island Conservation Trust and the Penguin Sanctuary. But without the financial inflows from the shark business Chivell had to take stock and diversify to whalewatching to keep his boat afloat. John: And the impact on your business? It has been 5 or 6 weeks now, is it becoming a strain? Wilfred: it is becoming a real strain, yes. If this carries on for another week or two I have to reorganise my business. It cant carry on like that. At least I have a whale watching business and I can carry some of the responsibilities of the shark to the whale watching business. V/O When Great Whites sense danger from a new predator in the vicinity their natural response is to flee. Alison Towner: It is very much a flight response and of course we don’t really know now how long it will take for the white sharks to sharks to be returning to the area. V/O There has only ever been one recorded incident of a Great White being killed by an Orca. It was off the coast of California. Alison: The fact is that we have not observed the live predation events here so the only evidence really that we have to relate to is off the western coast of California where 2 orcas were filmed extracting a white shark’s liver and in that situation what they sort of did was to bump it until they asphyxiated it and then they removed its liver. V/O Just a few days after we left Gansbaai several Great White sharks were again spotted in the bay. For now business is back on its feet but with irregular sightings becoming more common, will the shark cage diving business be able to sustain itself? Alison Towner: I just try and remain optimistic and I hope the natural balance will return. If it doesn’t we may as human beings really consider our impact on the ocean and what we can do to change that. ___________________________________________________________________________ PROMOS: 10sec unmixed promo: Shark cage diving is a major tourist attraction for both local and international visitors in the Western Cape but what happens when the sharks go missing. We travel to Gansbaai to investigate. 4 seconds up audio Wilfred Chivell: 386 - 02;03;42;00 If this carries on for another week or two I will have to reorganise my business. 30 seconds visuals 10 second mixed promo: Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry keeping the town of Gansbaai on the map. But what happens to business when all the sharks disappear? 15 second mixed promo: V/O Gansbaai is seen as the Mecca of Great White Sharks, but when four dead carcasses are found on the beach in one week a new reality sets in. Alison Towner: 416 - 00;02;55;05 The initial feeling there is complete and utter shock. You don’t expect to see something of that size washed out on the beach. 15 second mixed promo V/O For the first time in history the sharks of Gansbaai disappeared for a total of ten weeks bringing a multi-million rand industry to a standstill. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Shark cage diving is a multi-million rand industry keeping the town of Gansbaai on the map. We find out why for the first time in history are the shark nowhere to be seen.otry rthe
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Shark cage diving attracts tourist from across the world to Gansbaai. Seen as the mecca of the Great White Sharks, Gansbaai is a unique spot for the Great Whites where food is readily available from the two small islands eight kilometres away. Sixteen years ago the first shark cage diving operator opened shop. Today there are eight operators running 3 boat trips every day. Until February this year shark cage diving generated in excess of R1 600 million every day. Recent sightings of a pair of Orcas and five dead sharks washed out on the beach has brought this industry almost to a halt. Studies have shown that the sharks now fear for their safety and have moved to safer waters. What does the future hold for Gansbaai and the shark cage diving boat operators and what has the economic impact been on every business, from the one man operator to the large operators who is have used this form of eco-tourism to fund valuable scientific and marine research.
metadata.Summary: Gansbaai is the shark capital of the world for the Great Whites. With an estimated population of 1,500 sharks moving between the Cape waters and Mozambique, it was found that the majority of the sharks remained all year round in the Gansbaai waters. To study their movement in more detail, 38 Great White Sharks were tagged in 2012 with high tech satellite tags by a team of local and international marine biologists. They found the reason why so many Great White sharks are found around Gansbaai is due to the abundance of energy rich food readily available. Eight kilometres off the coast of Gansbaai a strip of sea between two small islands that forms the perfect breeding ground for seals and penguins, two key food sources of the Great White shark’s diet. Each year roughly 60 000 seal pups are born on Geyser Rock island and on Dyer Island the penguins are protected as part of ongoing research studies.
metadata.Further information: With almost a hundred percent guarantee of seeing these formidable creatures in their natural habitat, operators were able to sell tours with a smile. That is, until a few months ago when two things happened: the Great Whites went missing and at the same time Orcas, or Killer Whales were spotted in the bay. Killer Whales are rare visitors to these waters and never in recorded history have the Great Whites been so allusive. Instead of the guaranteed shark sightings, the cage dive boats started returning to land with disappointed tourists on board and even refunding a portion of the fee they pay to see the Great Whites. Then Alison Towner, a marine biologist who has been studying the Great Whites of Gansbaai for the last decade and was part of the tagging expedition in 2012 got a call from a local to tell her about a dead shark he found on the beach in Gansbaai. To her shock she found that it was one of the females that was tagged in 2012. But this was not the end. Within a matter of weeks, the same incident occurred four more times. A Great White found dead on the beach. The common denominator was that in each case only the shark’ liver was ripped from the carcass. “It is the first time in recorded history that we have seen something like this. Five identical cases of sharks found dead on the beach with its livers missing.” Alison identified three females of 4,9 meters and two males of 3,6 and 4,5 meters from the database tagging system. With the help of a team of experts, including dr. Malcolm Smale, Alison was granted permission by the Department of Environmental Affairs to dissect the sharks. The Great White sharks have only one natural predator, the Orcas, or Killer Whales as they are sometimes referred to. The Orcas are part of the dolphin family and will feed on their own, as well as sharks, baby sperms whales, seals, penguins and large fish. The only part of a shark that the Orcas are interested in, is the rich liver and sometimes the heart. With no previously recorded attacks of the Orcas on the Great Whites in this area, the theory is that the unsuspected sharks have now become easy prey for the sharks of Gansbaai. For Alison and the team of experts, they made history as it is the first time worldwide that Great Whites have been dissected after an Orca predation and it is also the first scientific observation of Orca killings on the Great Whites of South Africa. But who pays for the science that takes place behind the scenes of marine biology? Tourists. Through eco-tourism, Marine Dynamics, the largest cage diving operator is able to employ 90 full time staff, including Alison’s salary, several other marine biologists, researchers, interns from across the globe, chefs who cook the meals for the tourist, and so the list goes on and on. From the local B&B’s who provides accommodation for overnight tourists to the butcher selling the meat to the restaurants, to the small micro-enterprises like Martina who owns Sea View Cleaners, and want to know “when must I come and clean the windows again?, there is an industry that survives entirely on the sightings of the Great Whites in Gansbaai. After a two day recci in Gansbaai and taking a trip myself out to Shark Alley, I witnessed the tangible disappointment of every single tourist on board who was hoping to see these magnificent creatures. They came from the Canary Island, Brazil, Switzerland, Germany, Missouri, to the far corners of Canada, each paying big money to come to the shark mecca of the world. There are only two other places worldwide where the Great Whites can be observed, but only in Gansbaai are tourist able to take a short trip out to sea and ‘with no previous experience’ and no scuba diving gear, are the young and old able to come within inches of the Great Whites. But as we speak, the shark cage diving industry is in trouble. Since February this year, the cage diving boats have returned time and again without a single sighting of the Great Whites. One operator has told us that she has only had 230 cage diving trips in one season with very few sightings of sharks compared to the same time last year where she made 780 boat trips, where almost every excursion was a guaranteed shark cage dive. On the window of the tourist shop it reads: Eight shark cage diving boats - three trips per day! That would mount to 40 people per boat paying R1700 per person. Times that by eight boats three times per day and this small postage stamp in the small town of Gansbaai generates R1,632.00 per day. Our story: In our story we will go out to sea, interview the tourists to find out what they think, speak to the marine biologist about the science behind what is happening and talk to the boat concession owners who have lost major revenue and in some instances had to close shop. We have footage of the necropsy and some visuals of the sharks during cage diving. However there is no footage available of a shark being attacked by an Orca as this is mostly happening at night. The story will be about the sharks moving away to safer waters and the direct impact it has had on the cage diving operators and the ripple effect on the industry as a whole.
